questions.q: According to the NCERT textbook, what percentage of water in India is polluted, and which two functions of the environment fail when this occurs?
questions.a: 70% of water in India is polluted. The two functions that fail are: (i) resource supply (clean water becomes scarce) and (ii) waste assimilation (pollutants exceed absorptive capacity). A wrong answer (e.g., "50% polluted" or naming "life sustenance" as a failed function instead of the first two) reveals the student has not internalised the textbook's causal chain: pollution → loss of supply/assimilation functions → life sustenance function compromised.

questions.q: The textbook states: "Water has become an economic commodity." Explain why this statement is economically precise, using the concepts of scarcity, rivalry, and excludability.
questions.a: Water became an economic commodity because pollution and depletion made it scarce (demand > supply at zero price), rivalrous (my use of clean water reduces your availability), and excludable (treatment plants, tankers, bottled water allow sellers to exclude non-payers). A wrong answer that says "water was always an economic good" or "government made it a commodity" misses the endogenous shift: environmental degradation altered the good's economic characteristics from non-rival/non-excludable (public good) to rival/excludable (private/toll good).

questions.q: The CPCB monitors 125 rivers. In a hypothetical stretch, BOD = 8 mg/L, DO = 2 mg/L, and total coliform = 50,000 MPN/100ml. Classify this stretch per CPCB criteria and calculate the percentage by which BOD exceeds the bathing standard (3 mg/L).
questions.a: Classification: Polluted (BOD > 3 mg/L and DO < 4 mg/L both violated). BOD exceedance = [(8 - 3) / 3] × 100 = 166.67%. A wrong classification (e.g., "moderately polluted" or using only BOD) or arithmetic error (e.g., 8/3 = 266%) reveals inability to apply the dual-criteria (BOD AND DO) and basic percentage-exceedance calculation used in board exam data-interpretation questions.

questions.q: Compare the pollution dynamics of the Ganga (main stem) and the Yamuna (tributary) using these stylised facts: Ganga receives 60% domestic sewage, 30% industrial effluent; Yamuna receives 80% domestic sewage in Delhi stretch, 15% industrial. Which river's pollution is more amenable to decentralised treatment (STPs) and why? Which requires stricter industrial regulation?
questions.a: Yamuna's Delhi stretch (80% domestic) is more amenable to decentralised STPs because domestic sewage is point-source, predictable in volume/composition, and treatable with conventional technology. Ganga's higher industrial share (30%) requires stricter effluent standards, common effluent treatment plants (CETPs), and zero-liquid-discharge mandates because industrial effluents are toxic, variable, and inhibit biological treatment. A wrong answer reversing the logic shows confusion between point-source (domestic) and toxic/heterogeneous (industrial) pollution management.

questions.q: Evaluate this policy proposal: "To solve groundwater depletion in Punjab, the government should ban paddy cultivation and mandate maize." Consider: (a) farmer income, (b) food security, (c) water saving, (d) political feasibility.
questions.a: The proposal saves water (paddy: 1,500-2,000 mm; maize: 500-800 mm) but fails on: (a) farmer income — paddy MSP procurement gives assured returns; maize lacks procurement infrastructure, (b) food security — Punjab contributes 40% of central rice pool; replacement reduces buffer stocks, (d) political feasibility — powerful farmer unions resist crop diversification without income guarantee. A better policy: incentivise direct-seeded rice (saves 20-30% water), promote basmati (export-oriented, less water), and guarantee maize MSP. A student who only cites "water saving" ignores the political-economy constraints central to Indian policy questions.

questions.q: Design a 3-step water accounting framework for a 500-ha canal command area in Maharashtra that tracks: (1) surface water delivery, (2) groundwater extraction, (3) crop water consumption. Specify the data sources, frequency, and one indicator to flag unsustainable use.
questions.a: Step 1: Surface delivery — from Irrigation Department's daily gauge readings at canal outlet (cusec-days/ha). Step 2: Groundwater extraction — from energised pumpset census × hours run × discharge rate (monthly). Step 3: Crop consumption — from remote sensing (evapotranspiration) × crop coefficient (fortnightly). Unsustainability indicator: Stage of Groundwater Extraction > 100% (extraction > recharge) for two consecutive years. A poor answer lists only "meter readings" without distinguishing surface/groundwater sources or omits the sustainability threshold used by Central Ground Water Board.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Water resources in the Indian economic context refer to the stock and flow of freshwater (surface water in rivers, lakes, reservoirs and groundwater in aquifers) that serve as productive inputs for agriculture, industry, and domestic use; water pollution is the degradation of water quality beyond permissible standards (BOD > 3 mg/L, DO < 4 mg/L for bathing) due to ______ discharge of organic, inorganic, and toxic pollutants, reducing the resource's assimilative capacity and imposing negative externalities on downstream users.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you live in a ______ on the banks of the Yamuna in Haryana.
Fill in the blank: Observe the transition from water as a free good (zero price, abundant supply) to an economic good (positive price, scarce supply) — the core concept from Section ______.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can: (1) interpret Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) water quality data (BOD, DO, coliform counts) to classify river stretches as polluted/non-polluted, (2) calculate the rate of groundwater depletion using stage of extraction formula, and (3) explain the opportunity cost of water pollution in terms of foregone.
